articles.title: Plus one Ring; Minus one Belt
articles.summary: This article discusses celestial highlights for July viewing, prominently featuring the discovery of a vast, faint, retrograde ring around Saturn, detected by Spitzer, which influences the moon Iapetus. It also reports the unexpected disappearance of Jupiter's Southern Equatorial Belt (SEB), making the Great Red Spot more distinct, and offers updates on other visible planets like Venus, Mercury, and Mars.

articles.title: Black Holes No Joke
articles.summary: Black holes, mysterious and influential cosmic objects, are difficult to observe directly, but astronomers are attempting to study them through gravitational waves. The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO) was built to detect these ripples in space-time, despite their extreme weakness and the challenge of terrestrial noise. While current LIGO has not yet made a definitive detection, an upcoming upgrade to Advanced LIGO around 2014 promises a thousand-fold increase in observation volume, aiming to finally reveal the inner workings of black holes.

articles.title: Getting to the Point
articles.summary: This article details various engaging astronomy educational activities conducted with students through Project ASTRO, such as comet making, alien design, and solar system modeling, showcasing positive student reactions and learning experiences. The author emphasizes the significant intrinsic rewards for amateur astronomers participating in these programs, highlighting student appreciation and the lasting impact of their efforts. It also serves as an appeal for more astronomers to join Project ASTRO, particularly in areas like San Jose, by addressing common objections and outlining the program's value.

articles.title: Observatory Fund
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) Board of Directors has dissolved its Observatory Committee and plans to redirect all Observatory Fund donations into the club's General Funds, having abandoned all plans for obtaining or constructing an observatory. This announcement serves as the final public notice, and the Board is actively seeking input from any donors regarding these plans.

articles.title: SJAA Yosemite Public Star Party 2010
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) is hosting its annual Yosemite Public Star Party from September 3-5, 2010, at Glacier Point in Yosemite National Park. Up to 30 participants will receive free admission and camping in exchange for hosting three public star parties over the weekend. Participants are expected to bring scopes, attend multiple events, and be prepared for rough camping conditions.

articles.title: The Last Month in Astronomy
articles.summary: The 'Last Month in Astronomy' highlights several key advancements, including the successful return of JAXA's Hayabusa spacecraft with potential asteroid samples and the first direct observation of an exoplanet's orbital motion. Research on Mars provided new insights into the absence of organics due to UV radiation and the discovery of non-acidic, habitable water environments in its past, while the detection of methane-eating bacteria on Earth opened possibilities for life on bodies like Titan. Additional milestones include NASA's Dawn spacecraft setting a velocity change record, SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket successfully launching, and the SOFIA airborne observatory achieving 'first light' for infrared observations.

articles.title: It Must Be Astronomical...
articles.summary: The 'It Must Be Astronomical...' article from the SJAA Ephemeris newsletter highlights the San Jose Astronomical Association's telescope loaner program and features a Q&A regarding the Sun's fate during the Milky Way-Andromeda collision. It provides a list of upcoming astronomical events and conferences, including the Golden State Star Party and SETIcon, alongside contact information for SJAA officers, staff, and details about the newsletter's publication.
